name: Aisha Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha Hansen, 43, and I operate a water cart at a large mine. I refill it, spray the haul roads to keep dust down, and report ruts before a truck hits them. I'm junior on the crew and still learning how much water each stretch needs; the senior operator checks my notes. My partner stocks shelves on evening shifts, and our two children are in school. The mortgage takes a big piece of our lower wages, and we have less than a month of expenses put away; I like keeping the roads safe, though the rotating shift means supper is often left warming for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small AI changes should be judged by whether they make the roads safer. My water cart still needs a driver who can see dust lift behind a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect this mild change to remove my cart shift. I do worry about a thin bank balance whenever my partner's shelf hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a paper road log and report each deep rut to the shift supervisor. I'd skip the children's paid cinema trip this month and put that money into the emergency jar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cart feels safe enough in this picture, but home doesn't feel comfortable. Last month my partner lost an evening shift and we moved a bill by four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a paper log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The radio is busy at changeover, and I need a record of which bend I sprayed. I hand it to the next driver so they don't start by guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the cinema?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can borrow a film and make popcorn at home. They would hear the truth. The house payment comes first this month.

fieldNote: She considers her **physical driving** stable here, but a recent lost household shift explains her anxiety.
Her careful **road log** reflects junior status and a wish to earn the senior operator's trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how the new dispatch plan deals with dust and ruts, not just trip times. I'd say a tested tool is worth trying if drivers can correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners may be fewer, and the rest of us may get shorter spray windows. I'm junior enough that a manager could call my hours flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the mine's route display with the senior operator after a supervised shift if it is offered. I'd ask the shift supervisor for a written record of any change to my weekly hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can work with a new display after someone shows me it works in the dust. A shorter roster would be harder to learn around than a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check on that display?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare its dry-road warnings with the places I saw dust at midday. I have used AI now and then to explain a term, but I would not let a phone choose the spray rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to if your hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner first, because evening shelf shifts and school pickup have to fit my roster. Then I'd ask the supervisor what work is still paid for next week.

Her worry centres on **paid hours** and coordinating school pickup with her partner's evening work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 could change planning, but a person still drives the cart for now. I'd want a firm notice before robot carts around 2031 take road work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is not long enough to clear our mortgage. At 45 I would still need pay, and the few nearby mines couldn't take every cart driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine about a paid road-maintenance apprenticeship this winter, if one is advertised. I'd keep my cart shifts through the first year after 2028 while people still operate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened when I count from the school calendar to the robot date. I will look at an apprenticeship, but I won't gamble the house on an unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why road maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already spot ruts and drains on my rounds, but I don't know how to repair them. A real apprenticeship would teach the tools and pay me while I learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could ask for more shelf hours, though the shop does not always have them. We would work out pickup before saying yes to a shift neither of us can cover.

feel: **Alarmed** by the short path from thinking AI to robots and possible lost wages.
S2.quote: I won't gamble the house on an unpaid promise.
fieldNote: She understands the **2028 office change** is earlier than the direct threat to cart driving around 2031.

steps.text: Apply for a paid road-maintenance apprenticeship if the mine advertises one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year lead should be used for proper instruction on roads and machines. I'd ask management to show families which cart runs might change by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031, with children older but still needing us. The extra time may let us build two months of savings, if both rosters hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put one small fixed amount from each pay into a separate emergency account starting this month. I'd apply for a paid grader trainee place if the mine offers supervised instruction next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like a path I could walk, even if it is uphill. The grader may be automated later too, so I would need the training to lead somewhere beyond one seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the cart while it still needs me and ask for training that includes road repairs, not only another control screen. My children would be teenagers then, so I'd check their school costs before agreeing to a training roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family help with costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could collect the children once in a while, but she has her own work. I would ask for a specific day, not build a whole plan on my sister's free time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years is enough time for a proper apprenticeship if the mine starts one soon. I'd want families shown the 2039 robot schedule before making promises about our futures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I could still have years of work ahead. My children may be grown by 2039, but the mortgage and our own living costs will not vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine training office this quarter about paid drainage and road-repair apprenticeships. I'd keep mortgage overpayments small and regular only when both household rosters are full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more able to act with a decade, and I would take a tested course even if I were older than the other trainees. I still would not call a road-repair trade safe forever after the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the apprenticeship to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want time with a crew fixing drains after rain, not just a certificate from a screen. If the work pays throughout training, I can show my children that learning later in life is normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine never offers a paid place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cart job while it lasts and ask a local road contractor whether they train adults on wages. I would not quit first and hope a vacancy appears.

S4.quote: I would not quit first and hope a vacancy appears.
fieldNote: The longer warning supports **paid practical training** and modest mortgage payments, subject to household shifts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A robot cart around 2031 could end my wage before I have finished learning another paid trade. A real apprenticeship with wages, a clear schedule for the cart routes, and enough notice to arrange school pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether training hours match family hours. A place that starts when my partner is at the shop and the children need collecting is only a place on paper.

headlineQuote: A place that starts when my partner is at the shop and the children need collecting is only a place on paper.
portrait: Aisha is a **43-year-old junior** water-cart operator who records dusty roads and ruts at a large mine.
Her partner's evening shelf shifts, two school-age children, a **mortgage**, and minimal savings make schedules as important as wages.
She uses AI **occasionally** and will try a proven tool with another operator beside her.
She seeks **paid practical training** in road maintenance and checks whether training hours fit school pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her only three years before robot carts could remove her paid driving work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, clear route dates, and training hours that allow school pickup would help her act.
